articles.title_orig: A painting went missing 20 years ago. Police tracked it down with the help of AI
articles.title_zh: A painting went missing 20 years ago. Police tracked it down with the help of AI
articles.content_orig:
Art theft is a global problem and police forces are struggling to keep on top of it. Now they are turning to AI software that snoop out the most cleverly hidden artworks.
During their routine visit to the annual antiquity fair in Parma , Italy, in October 2024, police officers busily snapped photos of the artworks as they walked between the stands. It wasn't art appreciation – it was detective work.
The images were uploaded to an internal database as the officers smiled at the vendors and wandered amid fist-sized bronze statuettes, patinated goblets, yellowing globes, and an endless assortment of oil paintings.
Just a couple of hours later, though, the police system flagged one of the snapshots with an alert signal: a painting of a young, fair-skinned woman wearing aquamarine and red, holding up a half-unravelled parchment scroll.
The next day, officers rushed to the scene and seized the painting for their art experts to take a second look. The scroll in the painting was now, indeed, giving the investigators reason to be suspicious, says Lt Col Salvatore Rapicavoli, of the police unit for the Protection of Cultural Heritage of Italy. "There was something off."
While Rapicavoli's team has specialised in tracking down stolen artworks nationwide for decades, he says that the novel, tailor-made artificial i ntelligence system they were testing at the fair has massively sharpened their craft. It has since allowed the team to detect stolen art more quickly and helped them to spot details beyond what the human eye can normally see.
"There has been an exponential increase in the number of hits," says Rapicavoli. Since its introduction in November 2023, the AI system has helped his team recover more than 300 large plundered paintings and statues, and more than 165,000 smaller coins, medals, letters, manuscripts, religious objects, stamps and cards worth more than a total of €203m (£170m, $226m). The advances in Italy – in technique and policy – have been paving the way for machine learning in art theft investigations worldwide , promising to revolutionise the global crackdown on art heisters.
And while a human would likely have glossed over that woman holding a parchment scroll at first glance – nothing but a couple of darker shadows looking off balance – the team now had an active investigation on their hands.
Since 1969, the Italian police have kept a database of looted cultural artefacts across the nation – everything from gigantic oil paintings ripped from church altars in the night to ancient Roman and Etruscan artefacts excavated illegally. The database – the largest in the world, constantly fed by reports from cultural police authorities and customs – contains more than one million items. Though only some of the entries have pictures of the original artefacts.
Historically, to find stolen artworks, Italian police routinely visited fairs, antique shops, and upscale art auctions and compared what they saw there with millions of records back in their offices, first in paper form, then digitised in an online database. One by one, they would look for matches in the online repository by searching keywords, querying with details like "painting of woman with scroll".
This was time-consuming and clumsy, though, says Rapicavoli. Even if a sale looked suspicious, an officer scrolling through hundreds of database photos for a match could often miss key details. And the quality of the original artefact photos left a lot to be desired. The images were often taken decades earlier, in black and white, far away, on someone's dining room wall and littered with light blowouts, obscured areas, or extreme contrast.
"I asked myself how technology could get around this problem," says Rapicavoli, an IT engineer who joined the Italian police's stolen art team in 2013. "At least in the massive search-and-comparison phase."
In 2020, his team conceived the AI algorithm called the Stolen Works of Art Detection System (Swoads). "The machine doesn't get bored," says Rapicavoli. Crucially, it can match hidden visual fingerprints in the works – pairing similarities between shades of colour and rough silhouettes.
It can also spot segments of paintings that have been chopped up and rearranged – as is often the case with large altarpieces sold in separate slivers – or works that have been tweaked after being stolen. "Regardless of whether it makes sense or not, it recognises it because it's part of a whole that was stolen," says Rapicavoli. It can reconcile the art without truly knowing its meaning or content.
A manual search for a painting of a "woman with a scroll" in the stolen artworks database wouldn't have solved the case on Rapicavoli's hands. The keywords wouldn't have surfaced the painting stolen 20 years earlier, in which that same fair-skinned woman clutches a small white lamb and a palm branch instead of a scroll.
Because the AI had spotted the similarities in colour, pattern and set-up – irrespective of the missing scroll – it flagged it among millions of stolen artefacts despite the manner of its disguise. Once it fetched the source image it believed it resembled, the similarities to the human eye were immediately apparent.
In fact, a closer investigation confirmed that a 17th-Century, 1m-tall (3.3ft) painting of Saint Agnese had been looted from the small church of Virgo Potens in Sulmona, near Naples, over 500km (310 miles) from the Parma art fair, on the night of 11 August 2004. It had apparently then been painted over to appear less recognisable – the lamb now the scroll, and the halo and the palm branch erased to turn the Saint into a young pagan woman instead.
As the art trade moved from in-person auctions to online marketplaces, Rapicavoli's team was finding itself constantly playing catch-up with a flurry of new uploads across e-commerce platforms, social media, and even the dark web. Now Swoads can continuously crawl catalogues and new uploads day and night, constantly scraping the internet and comparing millions of images against a stolen-art database.
In 2026, for instance, the same software allowed his team in the Italian city of Turin to recover a painting by Filippo Palizzi, Riposo Della Pastorella (The Rest of the Shephardess), stolen from a modern art gallery in June 1972, in a robbery so severe the establishment remained shut down for over 30 years.
Although the painting had been missing for decades, lost in the backrooms of art markets and trade shows, one of its routine trawls of the internet spotted it for sale on an auction house website.
Still, AI isn't a silver bullet against art theft, says Carina Popovici, the co-founder of Art Recognition, a company using AI for art authentication. These systems answer a specific question: does this image match something reported stolen? They don't catch the thief, and they can't flag something that was never recorded, she notes. "The recovery still depends on investigators and legal cooperation," says Popovici. "I would call AI a force multiplier."
Timothy Carpenter, the former head of the FBI's Art Crime Team, and founder of Argus Cultural Property Consultants, a risk management and consulting firm, agrees. The software can't replace human analytical thought.
For one, there are still many technical issues to iron out. While the technology has become much better at recognising stolen art even from low-quality photographs, it still struggles with poor training data. Its recognition of 3D objects, too, is severely impaired – a vase photographed from the front in the theft report will likely not match a listing photographed from the back. Rapicavoli's team is already working to improve this.
And there are systemic issues: "You have to have a large team dedicated to nothing but chasing leads generated by the AI," says Carpenter – a luxury most law enforcement branches cannot afford. "The Italians have somewhere in the neighbourhood of 300 personnel assigned to their art crime unit. At its largest, the FBI had 24."

articles.title_orig: Golan calls on opposition bloc to form government with Arab parties
articles.title_zh: Golan calls on opposition bloc to form government with Arab parties
articles.content_orig:
Democrats party head Yair Golan on Wednesday morning called for Israel's opposition to form a government with the resurgent Arab parties in the next Knesset, arguing that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu lost the 2026 election with some 55 seats, compared to the opposition's 65.
"Netanyahu lost. I know how to count to 120. Sixty-five is more than 55. That's how Israeli democracy works. Period," the former IDF deputy chief of staff wrote on social media.
"We have no future here if we don't stop being afraid...We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes ," Golan added. "The voice of an Israeli citizen voting in Taybeh is worth exactly as much as the voice of an Israeli citizen voting in Givat Shmuel."
Arguing that the opposition has a majority along with Ra'am and the Joint List, Golan said that his bloc has a "responsibility and an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens."
Golan further argued that the opposition won a Zionist majority, saying that the prime minister "should substract 16 seats" belonging to non-Zionist, haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties in Shas and United Torah Judaism .
Later on Wednesday, Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen said on Wednesday that his party was ready to "pave the way for the ousting of the Netanyahu government."
"Against a government of bloodshed, against a politics of supremacy, racism, and exclusion, we offer a completely different alternative," he posted on X/Twitter.
"The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership, a true and equal partnership. No less than that, and no more than that," he added.
Earlier, in an interview with Army Radio, senior Joint List lawmaker Ahmad Tibi hinted at his faction's to sit with the opposition in a government. “The opposition bloc will be able to form a government if it has the courage. We are extending a hand and are ready to help," he said.
MK Gilad Kariv (The Democrats) said that Israel is in a "different political reality" the morning after the 2026 Knesset elections and called for the opposition bloc to work with Arab parties.
“The fully right-wing coalition has lost quite a few seats. It will most likely be unable to form a government in a similar configuration," he wrote on X/Twitter.
"The opposition has grown stronger, both in its representation of the liberal Jewish public and in its representation of the Arab public. A substantial majority, by a margin of hundreds of thousands of votes, voted against Netanyahu .
"A huge segment of the Israeli public – one that serves, works, contributes, and creates – expects us to make significant and fateful decisions about Israel’s future and to continue acting together, with the full understanding that Netanyahu and his partners must not be allowed to continue leading our country down the destructive path they have taken over the past four years," he concluded.
This follows projections that two Arab parties, Ra'am and the Joint List, will win six and 11 seats, respectively, according to data from the Central Elections Committee (CEC).
The opposition bloc , comprising Yashar, B’Yachad, Yisrael Beytenu, and the Democrats, is expected to enter the Knesset with 49 seats, according to data from the CEC.
CEC data shows that Golan's Democrats is projected to win eight seats in the 2026 elections.

articles.title_orig: A US cruise ship suspends a global voyage in Asia due to fuel costs, stranding 200 passengers
articles.title_zh: A US cruise ship suspends a global voyage in Asia due to fuel costs, stranding 200 passengers
articles.content_orig:
A U.S. cruise ship on a residential world voyage has suspended its operations in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to abandon their homes
PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- A U.S. cruise ship on a residential world voyage suspended its operations in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to abandon their floating homes.
The Odyssey set sail two years ago on a three-year voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel.
The Florida-based company said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 has recently reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia during the war in Iran. Villa Vie Residences said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surge in fuel costs.
“We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses,” it said. “Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees" while it tries to restructure.
Sihanoukville Autonomous Port said in a statement last week that the ship docked on Oct. 23 for a five-day visit. It was to head to Vietnam but remained in the port Wednesday.
The ship carried 203 passengers with 15 nationalities, mostly Americans, and 156 crew members. It had a capacity of 650 residents.
Passengers have been told to leave the ship, but the crew's status was unclear.
The Odyssey had a confirmed itinerary into November 2027. The company planned for a second residential cruise ship to enter service in early 2029, but the statement on the suspension of the Odyssey's voyage did not address the second ship.
This version has corrected the date when the voyage was expected to end from 2030 to 2027.

articles.title_orig: Ten people confirmed dead in high-speed Spain train crash, local media report
articles.title_zh: Ten people confirmed dead in high-speed Spain train crash, local media report
articles.content_orig:
At least 10 people have been killed in a collision between two trains in the Spanish province of Toledo, it was reported on Wednesday.
The high-speed trains collided shortly before 9:15 a.m. local time (4:15 a.m. ET), when emergency services were deployed to the scene.
Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha, told Spanish broadcasters that the incident had resulted in at least 10 deaths.
Authorities said they would open the town of Urda's sports hall to provide assistance to those affected, with an Advanced Medical Post being set up at the site of the crash to triage the injured, provide medical care and transfer those requiring further treatment to hospitals. It is currently unclear how many people suffered injuries.
Railway infrastructure manager Adif is investigating the sequence of events surrounding the accident, Spanish news agency EFE reported on Wednesday.
Adif said in a post on X on Wednesday morning that traffic on the Madrid to Andalucía high-speed line had been interrupted due to a collision between two trains.
Newspaper El Pais reported that officials fear the number of confirmed fatalities may rise, with sources telling the outlet that Wednesday's collision could have a worse outcome than a high-speed crash in southern Spain that killed 45 people earlier this year.
"We don't have a figure, but it's going to be a major tragedy," Spain's Health Minister Mónica García told a television news station, according to El Pais.
Officials currently do not know for certain what caused the collision on Wednesday, but local reports said initial analyses pointed to human error. Government sources told El Pais that it appeared an Adif operator made a mistake when railway signaling systems failed. The systems are automated, but they rely on manual operation when signals fail.
The trains involved were operated by AVE and Iryo, according to local media, with at least two carriages said to have fallen down an embankment after the crash. More than 500 passengers were on board the two trains, El Pais said.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said in a post on X that he was "shocked" by the accident.
"Emergency services are working on the ground to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations," he said, according to a translation. "My affection, solidarity, and support to all the victims and their families."
Sanchez's political future will be tested in a snap election next month, which he called following widespread unrest over Spain's housing crisis.
Santiago Abascal, leader of the far-right Vox party — which is expected to make gains when Spain goes to the polls — pointed the finger at Sanchez's government over the train accident on Wednesday.
"Tragedy again. Rage again over the neglect, the ruin, and the betrayal suffered by the Spanish people," he said in a post on X.

articles.title_orig: Researchers Propose New Irrigation to Balance Water Conservation, Food security in China
articles.title_zh: Researchers Propose New Irrigation to Balance Water Conservation, Food security in China
articles.content_orig:
A new study shows that China may better balance water conservation, food security and investment returns by adopting more efficient irrigation strategies, and expanding irrigated farmland only where conditions are optimal.
The study, published in the journal Nature Food, was led by researchers at the Institute of Atmospheric Physics (IAP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Hohai University and Xiamen University, in collaboration with several other Chinese and international institutions.
As rising temperatures and droughts put more pressure on food production systems, irrigation is becoming more important for farmers adapting to climate change. But expanding irrigated farmland further burdens already limited water supplies. The researchers therefore look for ways to save water, protect cereal production and improve investment returns all at once.
The team examined 42,190 county-level agricultural statistical records, 3,576 household socioeconomic survey responses and 2,230 irrigation technology comparison trials. It also focused on China's three staple crops: maize, wheat and rice.
The study found that China's agricultural irrigation underwent a significant technological transition between 2010 and 2022. In 2010, earthen-channel water delivery and flood irrigation were still widespread. By 2022, these inefficient practices had declined substantially, while water-saving technologies had become more common. However, the pace of change varied widely across crops and regions.
Wang Jinxia, a professor at Hohai University in east China's Jiangsu Province, said upgrading irrigation and water-saving technologies has long been a key part of China's farmland water conservancy investment.
Wang explained that at the current rate of technology adoption, irrigation water use per area for the three staple crops is projected to fall by only 9.4 percent to 16 percent by 2030. This projected reduction would fall short of the 25.5 percent water-saving target set by the national agricultural sustainable development plan for 2015 to 2030. The plan sets a cap of 373 cubic kilometers on national agricultural irrigation water use by 2030.
The study showed that deploying the most efficient irrigation technologies across all existing irrigated areas could more than meet the water-saving target. However, even such widespread upgrades would not be enough to offset possible crop yield losses caused by future climate change, posing risks to food security.
The researchers therefore proposed a new approach: first improve water-use efficiency in existing irrigated areas, and then, within water resource constraints, use the water saved to convert some rainfed farmland into irrigated farmland. The strategy aims to reduce the adverse effects of future climate change.
The study also found different optimal strategies for the three crops. For maize, the preferred approach is to adopt more advanced irrigation technologies while moderately expanding irrigated areas. For wheat and rice, less expansion is needed, and medium-efficiency water-saving technologies in newly developed irrigated areas could be enough to ensure food security under future climate conditions, meet water-saving policy targets and maximize investment returns.
Zhang Tianyi, a senior scientist at IAP, said the real question policymakers need to answer is which crops need irrigation, where irrigated area should be expanded, by how much, what technologies should be adopted and whether the investments are economically viable.
He noted that previous studies had largely focused on projecting changes in irrigated areas without fully accounting for interactions among irrigation technologies or between existing and newly developed irrigated areas.
"By integrating multi-source data and developing a new analytical framework, the study aims to provide more actionable scientific evidence for these specific investment decisions," he said.
The researchers emphasized that irrigation is not the only solution. Agricultural production is also influenced by crop variety breeding, cultivation management, land management scale and other factors. Irrigation investment should therefore be coordinated with the development of stress-tolerant crop varieties, climate-resilient cultivation practices and the construction of high-standard farmland.
Chen Huang, a researcher from Xiamen University in east China's Fujian Province, said the study drew on three independent datasets collected through different survey and research approaches. Despite their different sources, the model was able to capture the decline in agricultural irrigation water use and the improvement in irrigation productivity in China over the past decade.
"Future research will further incorporate agricultural policy and economic factors such as farmland consolidation and changes in agricultural commodity prices to refine the assessment of irrigation investment," he said. (Xinhua)

articles.title_orig: China Spaceplane CSSHQ: 3 Missions, 8,500 kg [2026]
articles.title_zh: China Spaceplane CSSHQ: 3 Missions, 8,500 kg [2026]
articles.content_orig:
A new Ars Technica report argues that China’s spaceplane cannot hide in low-Earth orbit , and the claim lands at a moment when the program is drawing more public attention than at any point since its first flight in September 2020. The vehicle at the center of the story carries the official name “reusable experimental spacecraft.” Its Chinese name is Chongfu Shiyong Shiyan Hangtian Qi, shortened to CSSHQ.
The headline framing is punchy, but the public record is more modest. The Secure World Foundation describes the CSSHQ as a technology demonstrator and experimental vehicle. Public listings show launches in September 2020, August 2022 and December 2023, with a fourth mission recorded for February 2026. The secrecy implied by the word “top-secret” is something we cannot confirm from the sources we retrieved. That gap between headline and evidence is the real story, and this analysis walks through both sides.
Why does it matter for a hardware audience? Because a reusable vehicle that releases small satellites, flies close to them and comes home is a test bed for sensors, guidance computers, thermal protection and launch integration. It also arrives while commercial launch cadence is climbing fast, as our report on SpaceX tying the California launch record with its 71st Vandenberg flight shows. More traffic in low orbit means more eyes on every object up there, including this one.
Don't miss new tech stories on Google
Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.
Start with the cleanest layer of facts. The Secure World Foundation, a space policy nonprofit, calls the CSSHQ a technology demonstrator. Its assessment says the craft deployed a small satellite during each of its first three missions, and that it performed limited rendezvous and proximity operations with the satellites it released. Those statements form the backbone of everything public about the program.
The mission list is just as plain. Public records place the first three launches in September 2020, August 2022 and December 2023, all on the CZ-2F/T launch vehicle. A search record adds a fourth mission in February 2026. A catalog entry lists an orbit of 332 km by 348 km, inclined 50.20 degrees, for a spacecraft of 8,500 kg.
Now the other layer. Several details that circulate around this story are unconfirmed in the retrieved sources. They include the “top-secret” label, the claim that the vehicle “can’t hide,” and any specific photograph, photographer or commercial satellite imaging event from 2024. Outlets including Ars Technica, TWZ, The Aviationist, Popular Science and Starlust.org have covered the story. The imaging details surfaced in one outlet’s search result, and none of the other retrieved sources confirms them. We treat them as reported claims, not settled fact.
This distinction shapes how a careful reader should handle the China spaceplane story. A craft can be tightly controlled by its operator and still be openly cataloged, because tracking networks log anything that reaches orbit. “Secret” often describes the mission goals, not the existence of the object. That reading fits the evidence far better than the dramatic version.
The acronym CSSHQ comes straight from the Chinese name, Chongfu Shiyong Shiyan Hangtian Qi, which translates as reusable experimental spacecraft. The English phrase matters. It tells you that the program office, at least in public, frames the vehicle as an experiment first. Wikipedia’s entry on the Chinese reusable experimental spacecraft collects the public mission history, and the Secure World Foundation uses the same experimental label.
Press and social media often call it a spaceplane. That shorthand is understandable, since the concept resembles a small winged orbiter that launches on a rocket, spends time in orbit and returns to land. But the fact sheet we rely on does not confirm the vehicle’s dimensions, wing geometry or landing method. We can say that the program describes a reusable spacecraft. We cannot responsibly describe its shape.
What about the owner? The retrieved sources do not name a manufacturer or a formal operator. They also do not state a price, a payload capacity or detailed mission objectives beyond the experimental role. Analysts who fill those blanks are drawing inferences. Some inferences are reasonable, yet none is a documented fact.
For readers who track the broader hardware industry, the naming is a useful clue about intent. A program that stresses reuse is chasing lower cost per flight and faster turnaround, the same pressures driving commercial rockets. A program that stresses experimentation is gathering data, not fielding a service. The CSSHQ sits firmly in the second camp for now.
Four launches over roughly five and a half years is a slow cadence by any standard. The gaps between the first three missions run close to two years, then about sixteen months. The fourth entry, dated February 2026, follows the December 2023 flight by a little over two years. That is arithmetic on public listing dates, not a claim about internal schedules.
Look closely at the fourth row. The verified material confirms the launch vehicle only for the first three missions. It does not confirm whether the February 2026 flight used the same rocket, whether it released a satellite, or whether the vehicle has landed. Any article that states those points as fact goes beyond the evidence we can verify.
That limit matters because the most dramatic claims in circulation attach to the newest flight. Reports of maneuvers and repeated releases deserve attention, and readers should check the outlets directly. Still, a responsible summary separates the three well-documented missions from the one whose details remain thin.
One entry in the Skyrocket space catalog record for the CSSHQ lists an orbit of 332 km by 348 km, with an inclination of 50.20 degrees, for an 8,500 kg spacecraft. Treat it as one catalog entry, not a universal description of every mission. The retrieved material does not say which flight the figures belong to, and orbits change over a mission.
Even so, the numbers carry useful information. A perigee of 332 km and an apogee of 348 km put the craft in a nearly circular orbit, with just 16 km separating the low and high points. The mean altitude works out to 340 km. That is deep in low-Earth orbit, where residual atmosphere drags on any object and where operators need propulsion to hold altitude over long stays.
The last three rows are our own calculations, labeled as such. At a mean radius of about 6,711 km from Earth’s center, standard Kepler math gives a period near 91 minutes. That means roughly 15 to 16 laps around the planet each day. The 50.20 degree inclination means the ground track sweeps latitudes up to about 50 degrees north and south, which covers most of the populated world.
The Ars Technica headline rests on a physical truth that has nothing to do with this one program. Objects in low orbit move fast, cross the sky in minutes and repeat their passes on a predictable schedule. Anyone with the right sensors can log them. Radar networks, telescopes and radio receivers all work on this problem, and low orbits are the easiest to observe because the targets are closest.
An 8,500 kg craft is big. If the catalog mass is right, it outweighs many commercial satellites several times over, and size helps ground trackers. Large objects reflect more sunlight and return stronger radar echoes. Sensor technology on the ground keeps improving too, which we saw in our look at counter-drone tests covering four sensor types , where radar, radio-frequency, optical and acoustic detection each filled different gaps.
The word “hide” still deserves care. A tracker can see that an object exists and where it flies without learning what it does. Orbit data reveals position and maneuvers. It does not reveal payload contents, onboard software or intent. So the headline’s claim and the program’s secrecy can both be par

articles.title_orig: King acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins
articles.title_zh: King acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins
articles.content_orig:
King Charles III has begun his tour of the Caribbean by acknowledging the "great suffering of the past" as he faced calls for slavery reparations.
Speaking an event in the Bahamas celebrating local youth, the King said the country's culture was "born out of darkness", and it was "only right" to acknowledge historic injustices.
His nine-day tour will culminate in the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), where the King has confirmed leaders will discuss the region's legacy of slavery.
The visit, his first as monarch, comes in the wake of renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit.
Prior to the trip, Buckingham Palace said the King would not shy away from "colonial legacy" and the impact of the slave trade during his visit but, in line with the UK government position, he will not apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade or offer reparations.
Upon his arrival on Tuesday, the King met Governor General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and its Prime Minister Philip Edward Davis, before speaking with members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as he inspected a guard of honour.
King Charles, wearing sunglasses and a grey suit, was then met with cheers as he arrived for his first engagement at a youth rally at Clifford Park - where he attended  independence celebrations for the Bahamas as Prince of Wales in 1973.
The young people in the crowd had been given time off school for the event. "It's my first time seeing him in person out of TikTok so he's out there, it's cool," one student told the BBC.
A small group of protesters gathered close to the rally shouting "pay us what you owe us" and "return artefacts you've stolen."
The group of around a dozen protesters was kept outside the main venue as they called on the King to help change the UK government's position on apologising and offering reparations.
"He's a man of influence. The Crown still has influence. And if they do not do it then we will become a republic and we will turn our backs on England if you do not show respect to the former colonies," said one protester, Sharon Purcer-Cooper.
During his speech in Nassau, the King acknowledged his 50-year-long commitment to fighting climate change and highlighted the challenges faced by low-lying Caribbean islands, saying that "our world cries out for healing".
He went on to call on young people at the rally to "take up the sacred task to play your part" as "in years to come, this will be surely be the measure of every person - how they answered the call to care for planet earth - the source of our life, our prosperity and our security".
The King resumes engagements in the Bahamas on Wednesday, where he will hear how vulnerable the low lying islands of the Caribbean are to climate change.
He will also learn more about the Bahamian tradition of Junkanoo - a cultural festival and street parade.
Buckingham Palace said opportunities for the King to reflect on the legacy of the slave trade will be built into the schedule of his nine-day tour of three Caribbean countries with visits planned to memorials and other places of reflection and remembrance.
A spokesperson for the palace told the BBC that the King's programme on the tour "will primarily focus on shining a light on the many modern partnerships and opportunities for the future", specifically those which are "having a transformative effect on the region".
For the King, the spokesperson added, the "tour is both a new journey but also the continuance of a lifelong one, in which he has sought to engage, understand and educate about the most shameful aspects of our past".
Those themes will be reflected by the King through the nine-day visit, the palace said.
The visit has been planned alongside the governments of the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda with an emphasis on honouring the past but also looking forward to the ambition and possibility for future generations.
The King will move to Guyana later this week where his engagements will focus on the environment and biodiversity.
He will then visit Antigua and Barbuda, where he will be joined by Queen Camilla, for the CHOGM and his keynote speech as leader of the Commonwealth.
The biennial summit will bring together leaders of 56 Commonwealth countries to address shared challenges and advance cooperation.

articles.title_orig: It can be lonely at the top. And that’s just how China’s leader likes it
articles.title_zh: It can be lonely at the top. And that’s just how China’s leader likes it
articles.content_orig:
Last week Beijing’s deputy mayor was meeting with Walmart CEO John Furner and encouraging American companies to invest in the Chinese capital. Now he has vanished from public life, the latest to be swept up in an anti-corruption campaign that has ensnared a galaxy of China’s talent: a former top judge, a spy chief, dozens of military generals – and even officials tasked with rooting out graft in the People’s Republic.
In hushed tones across China party officials are wondering who is next, as the purge continues to reach into the highest echelons of the ruling Communist Party and has even toppled those seen as being close to leader Xi Jinping.
The only person who doesn’t need to worry about his future is Xi himself.
Unlike US President Donald Trump , who is currently battling to save his party’s fortunes at the midterm elections and is constitutionally barred from serving more than two terms, Xi’s rule over the aspiring superpower and world’s second-biggest economy has never looked more secure.
He will take that confidence into a high-level closed-door meeting of more than 200 of the party elite in Beijing this week that is all set to further boost his authority – and his signature anti-corruption drive. Attendance at this meeting will be at a historic low – because of the anti-corruption measure.
The meeting is being particularly closely watched because it is held just a year before an even more important gathering of Communist Party leadership next fall where Xi is expected to engineer for himself an unprecedented fourth term.
The years-long anti-corruption campaign has ensured there are few, if any, figures or factions who could stand against him.
Since Xi, 73, came to power over 14 years ago millions of rank-and-file officials have been purged. In 2022, Xi called to “turn the blade inward” to investigate those tasked to enforce discipline themselves.
But he’s still not satisfied.
Earlier this year he told party cadres that the corruption problem “remains grave” and warned that there were still many “two-faced people” in the party. The war against graft, he promised, would be a “never-ending struggle.”
In recent months, the speed and scale of the anti-corruption drive have reached levels unseen in decades.
According to official data from the party’s Central Commission of Discipline Inspection (CCDI), between 2012 and 2022, over 500 ministerial-level officials have been probed, later convicted, removed from their posts, and expelled from the party for corruption.
In just the past three years, more than 410 officials have been purged.
Some of those purges have reached places that were once considered untouchable.
The party’s top military decision-making body, the usually seven-member Central Military Commission is now down to only two members – one of those being Xi himself . The 24-member politburo - the party’s top echelon - is down to only 21 members.
Over the past three weeks, ahead of the Beijing meeting, the CCDI has been sending out near daily updates of arrests, new probes and expulsions from the party.
The news that Huang Qifan was being probed sent shockwaves through political circles.
Huang was a longtime mayor of the megacity of Chongqing, known as a consummate political survivor who had served under six different secretaries of the Communist Party – and seen two of them go to jail, including a former rival of Xi.
In retirement, Huang was prolific at conferences and on TV, giving his takes on the Chinese economy.
Since his downfall, those who knew Huang have rushed to scrub all mention of their former well-connected friend and colleague from their social media accounts – a common practice in China.
For Beijing deputy mayor Xia Linmao, the purge came suddenly. Only days before, state TV showed him at a meeting with Walmart’s Furner and a slew of other US executives, nodding and taking his notes as his boss invited the group to do more business in Beijing.
Others simply vanished from public view, with news of their investigation not appearing for months, like Ma Xingrui, an aerospace engineer turned senior party official who once ran the vast western region of Xinjiang. The authorities announced an investigation into him in April – after he had not been seen in public for five months.
Being officially investigated for corruption almost always spells the end of a political career in China, with guilty officials kept from the public eye even after they have served their sentences.
And in recent months, authorities have shown they are willing to use capital punishment to enforce the party line, even for those who were once trusted aides of Xi.
In May, two former defense ministers, Wei Fenghe and Li Shangfu were given suspended death sentences, with a two-year reprieve , after being convicted of bribery.
Years of purging has left a generation of younger officials with fewer seniors left who can provide patronage, protection and career advancement, and the situation where the most powerful person in China does not have an apparent heir , in a break from his predecessors.
And for some, that’s just fine.
Deng Yuwen, a former deputy editor of the Study Times, the official publication of the party’s top training institute, told CNN that “now younger people all listen to Xi, isn’t this better? At this point, I don’t think Xi needs to worry about whether someone is already his trusted aides. “
“Whoever he promotes will become his loyalist,” said Deng. “And he has enough time to make someone his trusted loyalists.”

articles.title_orig: Global stock markets rise as investors continue to bet on AI
articles.title_zh: Global stock markets rise as investors continue to bet on AI
articles.content_orig:
CNBC's Jim Cramer warned Tuesday that investors may be getting ahead of themselves by declaring the artificial intelligence trade back on track.
AI-related stocks rallied for a second straight session, fueled by renewed enthusiasm for chipmakers after a group of banks and Blackstone announced $63 billion in financing for Anthropic to purchase Broadcom's computing hardware. The gains followed Monday's rally, sparked in part by Anthropic's S-1 filing . But Cramer cautioned the renewed optimism doesn't resolve the pressures facing the data center trade, which was hit hard late last week .
"I'm pleased that people feel so comfortable that tech is all good to go because there is money flowing back in," the " Mad Money " host said. "I don't think that's a reason to call all clear. I think it's a reason to look at other sectors in the economy."
Cramer's skepticism centers on three lingering risks.
First, Cramer remains concerned about smaller AI infrastructure companies, known as neoclouds, that are taking on significant debt to fund the data center build-out. Rising interest rates have intensified worries about their ability to sustain those borrowing costs. Cramer singled out CoreWeave , whose bonds have yielded as much as 15% , along with Nebius and Iren . Despite an almost 8% rebound in CoreWeave shares Tuesday, he warned that fresh negativity around CoreWeave could emerge.
"I have learned that after every positive story about anything in the data center, there will be a plethora of negative stories about something wrong, including Coreweave," Cramer said.
Second, Cramer questioned whether the Broadcom-Anthropic financing deal was as reassuring as investors believed. While the $63 billion package demonstrated that lenders were still willing to finance massive AI investments, Cramer raised concerns that Anthropic is borrowing money to buy Broadcom's technology, rather than paying for it with profits from its own business. "People don't seem to grasp that [Anthropic] got the money in the Broadcom-arranged financing deal to purchase equipment from Broadcom," he said.
Finally, Cramer said that Tuesday's calmer bond market could prove short-lived. Oil prices declined and the 10-year Treasury yield fell below 5%, easing some pressure on AI companies that need to borrow heavily to fund their data center investments. But those conditions could reverse, particularly with the Federal Reserve set to announce its latest interest rate decision Wednesday afternoon, followed by Chairman Kevin Warsh's post-meeting press conference. The midterm elections next week and potential flare-ups in the Middle East may represent additional sources of volatility.
"With the exception of Nvidia , these data center companies don't have a lot of money. So they have to borrow the money," Cramer said. "The rates are getting so high that the return is getting uncertain. That hasn't changed at all."
Cramer emphasized that he remains "an unabashed believer in the AI build-out." But until the industry's financing challenges ease, he isn't ready to declare the coast clear.

articles.title_orig: RAF Fairford Incident Was Coordinated By Man Acting for Iran, UK Prosecutors Say
articles.title_zh: RAF Fairford Incident Was Coordinated By Man Acting for Iran, UK Prosecutors Say
articles.content_orig:
London — Two men have been charged with serious security offenses in Britain after being arrested in connection with the incident last month near RAF Fairford, the air base in England that had been used by the U.S. military to launch strikes on Iran, the U.K. Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said Tuesday.
Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, both British nationals and London residents, were charged under the 2023 National Security Act.
Abdulkarim was charged with "assisting a foreign intelligence service" in September and "engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out U.K.-related activities."
The CPS said Essghir was charged with a national security offense after he "approached or was in the vicinity of a prohibited place and his conduct was for a purpose that he knew, or having regards to other matters known to him ought reasonably to have known, was prejudicial to the safety or interests of the United Kingdom."
Both men were arrested last week on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service in a suspected plot targeting the Fairford air base in England.
Abdulkarim was arrested by Counter Terror Police under the National Security Act last week, along with another 25-year-old man — a British-Iranian dual national who was released on bail pending further investigation.
Police are still investigating a suspected terror plot against Fairford after five men were initially detained on Sept. 27 near the base in western England. All five of those men were also released on bail, but police said they remained under investigation and would be monitored.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government believes Iran "played a part" in the incident at the base, which prompted the U.S. Air Force to remove all of its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford . The base had been home to U.S. long-range bombers for many years, and it was used during the war with Iran to launch strikes on the Islamic Republic.
Residents of a nearby town were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police and bomb-disposal experts searched the area on Sept. 27. They found gasoline in three vans that had been driven by the five initial suspects, parked close to an entrance to the base, but no explosives.
Iranian officials have said repeatedly that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets. The Iranian Embassy in London, however, said in a previous statement that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.
Police said Tuesday that six men remain free on bail in relation to the incident, four of whom were arrested on Sept. 27 — all U.K. nationals and London residents in their 20s — and two others who were detained subsequently, including the 25-year-old dual U.K.-Iranian national who was detained on Oct. 1.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs running close, but both shy of majority
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs running close, but both shy of majority
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that a right-wing government must be formed to ensure Israel’s long-term security, and that it cannot rely on coalitions with Arab parties “that are against our existence”.
He made the comments to supporters at his Likud party headquarters in West Jerusalem on Tuesday, several hours after polls closed in Israel’s legislative election and the early results were being announced.
With more than half of ballots counted , The Times of Israel projected Netanyahu’s bloc to win 56 seats and Gadi Eisenkot’s alliance, 49.
Neither is likely to secure a clear path to a governing majority.
Netanyahu said the “true results” were still one or two days away, while acknowledging that Likud was projected to become the “largest party in Israel”.
Likud was on track to win an estimated 27 seats to 21 for Eisenkot’s Yashar party, according to projections from Israeli Channels 12 and 13, giving Likud a clear lead over all others in the parliament.
Netanyahu also highlighted his achievements since taking office in his current term from 2022, which he sought to build upon.
“We worked wonders that changed the face of the Middle East. We eliminated [Mohammed] Deif, [Ismail] Haniyeh, [Yahya] Sinwar, [Hassan] Nasrallah, [Iranian Supreme Leader Ali] Khamenei,” he said.
“We established security zones deep inside Gaza, in Lebanon, in Syria. We removed an immediate existential threat that hung over us, the danger of immediate destruction. We struck the Iranian regime and brought it to the edge of the abyss. Iran is weaker than ever; Israel is stronger than ever.”
He said Israel had a “historical opportunity” together with United States President Donald Trump “to remove the existential threat of Iran once and for all”.
Alon Pinkas, a former Israeli ambassador who served as consul general of Israel in New York City, said the party that secures the majority of seats may have to seek an uncomfortable coalition deal in order to govern.
But he said opposition voters would not want the bloc to strike a deal with Netanyahu’s coalition.
Marwan Bishara, Al Jazeera’s senior political analyst, says Netanyahu attempted to put on a “brave face” about his party’s prospects during his speech in Jerusalem.
“It’s clear that he’s trying also to project a kind of success that he doesn’t merit. One, because he cannot form a coalition, but two, the idea that he is the largest party in Israel kind of hides the fact that this is the lowest Likud has reached since 2009.”
Political analyst Dan Perry told Al Jazeera that Netanyahu used his speech to “spin the situation as best as he could” after exit polls were released.

articles.title_orig: How China’s ancient capital staked a claim to the nation’s fastest export growth
articles.title_zh: How China’s ancient capital staked a claim to the nation’s fastest export growth
articles.content_orig:
Exports jumped 142.1 per cent in the first nine months of 2026, with computing equipment and integrated circuits making up more than 76 per cent
A booming semiconductor industry is helping drive a surge in trade in Xian, one of China’s ancient capitals, making it the country’s top performer by trade growth among provincial capitals and provincial-level cities for which data is publicly available.
The capital of western China’s Shaanxi province recorded a 115.5 per cent year-on-year surge in trade during the first nine months of 2026. Exports far outpaced imports, climbing 142.1 per cent.
Two product categories drove much of that export growth. Shipments of automatic data processing equipment and parts jumped 388.1 per cent year on year, while integrated circuits rose 251 per cent. Taken together, these categories accounted for 76.5 per cent of total exports.

articles.title_orig: Israel Election 2026 live updates: Netanyahu, Eisenkot caught in deadlock
articles.title_zh: Israel Election 2026 live updates: Netanyahu, Eisenkot caught in deadlock
articles.content_orig:
Fox News Digital speaks with three experts on Israel’s high-stakes election and the fight over Netanyahu’s political future. The election is set for Oct. 27, 2026.
JERUSALEM — Israel’s high-stakes election on Oct. 27 pits the longest serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, against the highly decorated retired Lt. Gen. Gadi Eisenkot. While fairly new to politics, Eisenkot has an impressive resume that could help him become the Jewish state's next leader.
According to a number of polls, Eisenkot's centrist political party, Yashar, has a narrow lead over Netanyahu's Likud. To form a government, Yashar or Likud will need to cobble together a 61-seat majority of parties to be able to form a new coalition government.
TRUMP SAYS NETANYAHU NEEDS TO BE RE-ELECTED, OR ELSE US WILL HAVE TO 'FINISH THE JOB’ AGAINST IRAN ALONE
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, speaks from behind a podium with a banner reading "Yashar with Eisenkot" during an event presenting the party's full candidate list ahead of October's general election on Sept. 7, 2026 in Rosh HaAyin, Israel. Eisenkot, a retired chief of the Israel Defense Forces, has emerged as the foremost challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. (Erik Marmor/Getty Images)
He was born in Tiberias in Israel’s north to a Jewish-Moroccan family who relocated to Israel’s southernmost city, Eilat, on the Red Sea when he was a toddler.
A career soldier, he opted to serve in the infantry. He was part of the elite Golani Brigade and reached the zenith of the military with his 2015 appointment to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) chief of staff in 2015 until 2019.
Yossi Melman, one of Israel’s most respected journalists on intelligence and defense reporting, told Fox News Digital that Eisenkot, "Is 100% a soldier. He is very brave and humble. He is an officer and gentleman."
Melman noted that when Eisenkot was chosen to be the next IDF chief of staff, he declined because he felt that then General Benny Gantz should receive the appointment. Melman asked, "How many people would do that? He was selected after Gantz. It shows his traits of modesty, honesty and not arrogant."
Melman said, "It is a miracle he is leading in the polls. He is the antithesis of a what a politician should be. He is not a great orator when you compare him to Netanyahu. He radiates honesty."
BENJAMIN NETANYAHU'S LEGACY AND POLITICAL FUTURE ON THE LINE IN ISRAEL'S OCT 27 ELECTION
Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot attends the Jerusalem Residents Conference on Aug. 12, 2026 in Jerusalem. Gadi Eisenkot, a retired chief of the Israel Defense Forces and current leader of the Yashar party, has emerged as the foremost challenger to Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of October's general election. (Erik Marmor/Getty Images)
Eisenkot’s Mizrahi background — Jews who originate from North Africa and the Middle East — would mean, if he prevails, that he would be the first Israeli Prime Minister of Moroccan origin. The Prime Minister’s office has been held by Israelis of Eastern European descent (Ashkenazi) since the rebirth of the Jewish state in 1948.
After Hamas invaded Israel on Oct. 7, 2023 and slaughtered over 1,200 people, including more than 40 Americans, Eisenkot joined Netanyahu’s war cabinet as a minister without portfolio.
Melman said Eisenkot "did not set any political conditions" and "his presence in the cabinet saved Netanyahu." After eight months of serving in the war cabinet, Eisenkot resigned, blaming the prime minister for failing to implement a comprehensive strategy.
The war against the Iran-backed terrorist movement Hamas took an enormous toll on the battle-hardened General Eisenkot and his family. Hamas killed his son, 25-year-old Master Sergeant Gal Eisenkot, in Dec. 2023. The terrorist organization also killed two nephews of Eisenkot. Netanyahu and his wife Sara said at the time that they were devastated by Gal’s death and Eisenkot was a "true hero."
ZIONISM EXPLAINED FROM ITS BIBLICAL ORIGINS TO THE REBIRTH OF THE STATE OF ISRAEL
Gadi Eisenkot, former Israeli army chief of staff and head of the Yashar party, is seen at the Black Arrow memorial site near Kibbutz Mefalsim during a visit to deliver a statement near the border with the Gaza Strip on Oct. 15, 2026, ahead of the Israel's legislative election. (Ilia Yefimovich/AFP via Getty Images)
Danny Orbach, a military historian from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, gave his take on the leading contender to replace Netanyahu. "I think his military record and his prospects as a national leader have both significant strengths and serious weaknesses. He bears considerable responsibility for shaping the IDF that existed on Oct. 7, 2023. And that was, paradoxically, both the army that proved capable of defeating Hezbollah, striking Iran and achieving unprecedented military successes in the extraordinarily difficult, tunnel-ridden battlefield of Gaza and the army that failed so miserably on Oct. 7."
He continued that, "Like other chiefs of staff, Eisenkot bears responsibility for the decisions that reduced the army's size and for the infamous ‘conceptzia’ [Hebrew word for concept] regarding Hamas. In that respect, I consider him just as culpable as Netanyahu."
Israel’s military, intelligence and political establishments bought into the ‘conceptzia’ that Hamas could be housebroken with massive infusions of economic aid. Hamas, however, was wedded to its radical Islamist ideology —the destruction of the Jewish state — and used the funds to advance its war aims.
Orbach noted that "I don't think most of Eisenkot's support stems from his energy, enthusiasm or even his political platform. My impression is that Eisenkot has emerged as the default ‘non-Bibi’ candidate, the politician who currently channels much of the camp's hopes and expectations."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Israeli Chief of Staff Gadi Eizenkot (L) give a press conference in Tel Aviv, on Dec. 4, 2018. Israel's army said today it has discovered Hezbollah tunnels infiltrating its territory from Lebanon and launched an operation to destroy them, a move likely to raise tensions with the Iran-backed group. (Jack Guez/AFP Via Getty Images)
Orbach added that "I also doubt that Eisenkot would have had the political determination to stand up to the Biden administration on such matters."
Netanyahu and former President Biden repeatedly clashed over Biden’s attempts to rope in Israel’s efforts to defeat Iran’s seven-front war against the Jewish state.
The military historian, however, noted that "I believe an Eisenkot government could address several of Israel's most urgent problems. It would remove Ben Gvir from power, confront the growing problem of Jewish extremist violence and terrorism in the West Bank, and begin repairing Israel's severely damaged international legitimacy."
Itamar Ben-Gvir is a controversial right-wing firebrand politician and the current minister of national security since 2022, who has outraged many Western European and foreign leaders with his heated rhetoric against the Palestinians.
TIMELINE OF DECADES-LONG ISRAELI-ARAB, PALESTINIAN CONFLICT
Former army chief Gadi Eisenkot attends the funeral for his son, First Sergeant Major Gal Meir Eisenkot, 25 years old, at the Herzliya cemetery on Dec. 8, 2023 in Herzliya, Israel. The Israel Defense Forces said the 25-year-old major, son of the cabinet minister and former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, died on Thursday in Gaza. (Dima Vazinovich / Middle East Images / Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images))
Eisenkot’s wife, Hannah, comes from an American Jewish family. U.S. General Joseph Dunford awarded Eisenkot the Commander of the Legion of Merit because of his "exceptionally meritorious service as chief of the General Staff of the IDF" and his "contribution to the strategic cooperation between the United States and Israel [that] will have a lasting effect on both countries," according to the Washington Institute, where Eisenkot served as a military fellow in 2019

articles.title_orig: ‘Awfully bleak’: why global carmakers keep losing ground in China’s vast market
articles.title_zh: ‘Awfully bleak’: why global carmakers keep losing ground in China’s vast market
articles.content_orig:
Carmakers are scrambling to revamp their strategies as China’s cash-strapped consumers turn away from expensive foreign brands
Global carmakers are searching for a way to survive in China’s cutthroat market, as they continue to lose ground to domestic competitors in a landscape that is increasingly tilting towards electric vehicles.
International auto brands from Volkswagen to Toyota saw their market share in the Chinese mainland slide once again in the third quarter of the year, as consumers turned away from expensive foreign cars amid an economic slowdown and the Iran war.
Foreign marques accounted for less than 30 per cent of deliveries over the period, down from 34.6 per cent a year earlier, as they delivered just 1.38 million cars to mainland customers, according to data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA).

articles.title_orig: Two Nordic leaders urge Putin to end Ukraine war in rare direct contact by Europeans
articles.title_zh: Two Nordic leaders urge Putin to end Ukraine war in rare direct contact by Europeans
articles.content_orig:
The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.
Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said the aim of the call had been to "convey messages directly regarding future negotiations" towards peace. An end to the conflict in Ukraine "will not be achieved through silence," Stubb said.
Neither side suggested the needle had been moved on ending the war, which began when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Although the Finnish leader said the conversation with Putin had been "frank and substantive," Støre added that there were "big differences in views" with Putin.
Several European leaders have recently shown willingness to engage with Russia directly, but both Stubb and Støre pointed out their initiative was taken in their capacity as neighbours of Russia, rather than on behalf of Europe as a whole.
"We've not set out to speak on behalf of anyone other than ourselves," Støre said.
Stubb added the call had been prepared in consultation with Ukraine and the US following a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the Nordic leaders and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo last week.
The first trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia talks since the start of the year are tentatively planned for early November in Abu Dhabi.
Zelensky later confirmed Stubb and Støre debriefed him after the call and said he was grateful for their "active support", while his Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been "the right approach".
Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the 90-minute call - held from Helsinki - to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.
Støre added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."
The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered.
Putin also reaffirmed to the Nordic leaders what he views as the "root causes" of the conflict - his frequent shorthand for Ukraine's desire to exist as a sovereign state.
"A fair long-term peace settlement is possible only if Russia's legal interests are taken into account fully and unconditionally", Putin said.
All three parties reportedly agreed to continue their direct phone communication.
There was no official EU reaction to the talks. The dialogue had not been coordinated with other European leaders, the Danish and Swedish prime ministers said. "I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo," commented Sweden's Ulf Kristersson.
Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had informed him that Europe's position on the upcoming talks in the United Arab Emirates was "moderately optimistic".
Relations between the US and Ukraine and its European allies have soured since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia, allowing Moscow to export oil to the America.
As the Trump administration's position on Russia has softened, several European leaders have said Europe should be trying to re-establish direct contacts with the Kremlin.
Stubb and Støre are the first European leaders to contact Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.
Soon after, Putin visited Alaska for a summit with Trump, and from then on Europeans were further sidelined from Ukraine peace talks. Moscow regularly mocks European leaders and accuses the EU of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons.
But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".
And although he said Moscow did not view Finland and Norway as speaking on behalf of Europe, on Tuesday Peskov conceded that Stubb and Støre's talks with Putin had been "very constructive and practical talks with the leaders of two key neighbouring states."

articles.title_orig: Here’s why the iPhone Duo’s hinge could be cracking the screen
articles.title_zh: Here’s why the iPhone Duo’s hinge could be cracking the screen
articles.content_orig:
Inside Apple’s first folding iPhone, contact with the delicate inner screen could cause a stress ‘hotspot.’
Inside Apple’s first folding iPhone, contact with the delicate inner screen could cause a stress ‘hotspot.’
Within hours of the iPhone Duo launch last Friday, people reported that the inner screen on some brand new foldable phones was already broken. The issue was similar across many photos shared on social media: some kind of issue or crack would appear in the middle of the screen above the hinge, with lines appearing on the right side of the display. On Monday, Apple acknowledged an “issue” and said it’s replacing damaged units, without going into much detail about how many broken phones have been reported so far.
So what’s actually going on?
Shahram Mokhtari, the lead teardown technician at iFixit, has actually taken apart the iPhone Duo and has a pretty good idea about the potential cause, telling The Verge that it’s due to an issue along the hinge, where a series of gears, springs, and joints work together to let the device close flat, while also trying to avoid creating a deeper crease by giving that screen space to bend more gently inside while it’s closed.
At the troublesome spot, it appears that the flexible inner screen is pushing up against a part of the hinge. That inner screen is already “extremely sensitive,” he says — if you took a pick or a sharp tool and poked at the edges of the screen, “you’re going to break that screen.” If you look at the pictures of damaged Duos on social media, there’s often a black spot where the damage is focused on the display, and that’s where the metal is hitting the screen, Mokhtari says.
You can see a visual representation of what Mokhtari is talking about in iFixit’s written and video Duo teardowns, which reveal where the hinge transitions, as the center hinge support makes space for a crossing flex cable, creating several edges that could ultimately be the culprit. The damage iFixit has been seeing is at a point where the center support bar might not always drop down far enough while the screen folds, possibly creating a stress “hot spot” between the flat bar and the bent screen inside a closed iPhone Duo.
At least one user with a broken Duo screen said they “felt something around the internal hinge” while showing it to a friend, kept opening it, and heard an “audible crack,” with the screen breaking. YouTuber CuriousHagi, who covered a Duo with dirt as part of a strenuous durability test, captured something similar on video , and the screen break appears in a similar spot. In a teardown video, CuriousHagi found that a part of the hinge that connects to the central bar had snapped .
Apple says the issue affects a “small number” of Duo units, and Mokhtari says that “In terms of numbers, we don’t know. Apple definitely has all the data here. And I suspect they know more than they’re telling us as well.” But he notes that because foldable screens are so delicate, a “certain number” of them will fail, as will a number of the hinges because they’re also “extremely complicated and delicate.” And while Apple isn’t recalling the Duos, “If three months from now, we’re still seeing the same kind of failure, then it’s a more widespread problem, and that might lead to a recall,” Mokhtari says.
Mokhtari points out that since this is the first generation of the iPhone Duo, it’s the first time Apple’s engineers are getting data on the hinge, and he says that “I guarantee you” Apple will redesign what’s at fault here for its next-generation foldable. He also notes that, generally speaking, “the phones do seem to be in people’s hands and people are using them, and they’re not running into any issues whatsoever.”

articles.title_orig: Taylor Farms recalls salad kits sold at H-E-B. See affected product
articles.title_zh: Taylor Farms recalls salad kits sold at H-E-B. See affected product
articles.content_orig:
Taylor Farms, the produce giant linked to the nation's largest-ever cyclospora outbreak that sickened more than 20,000 people this summer, has issued a new salad recall .
Taylor Farms of Dallas is recalling Backyard BBQ Chop Salad kits sold at H-E-B stores because they may contain allergens not properly listed on its packaging, according to an Oct. 27 notice from the Food and Drug Administration.
The recalled kits contain undeclared soy and tree nuts (almonds) that could trigger reactions in people with sensitivities or allergies. No adverse reactions have been reported to date.
Taylor Farms has been a consistent fixture in headlines this year after health officials identified iceberg lettuce grown by Taylor Farms de Mexico as the source of an unprecedented outbreak of cyclosporiasis, a gastrointenstinal illness caused by the parasite Cyclospora cayetanensis. The FDA declared the outbreak over in September and said on Oct. 2 that it had concluded its investigation, which found cyclospora was present in the environment where the lettuce was grown and processed. This latest recall is not related to cyclospora or Taylor Farms de Mexico.
The recalled kits were distributed at H-E-B stores in Texas and are packaged in a plastic bag. The product's best-by date and UPC are on the back of the package.
H-E-B Backyard BBQ Chop Salad Kit 13.4-ounce; UPC 041220300457, best-by Oct. 30, 2026.
Do not consume the recalled salad kits; either dispose of them or return them to the place of purchase for a refund, per the FDA notice.
Customers with questions may contact Taylor Farms at 855-455-0098.

articles.title_orig: China’s top-secret spaceplane can’t hide in low-Earth orbit
articles.title_zh: China’s top-secret spaceplane can’t hide in low-Earth orbit
articles.content_orig:
A winged Chinese spacecraft bearing a strong resemblance to the US military’s X-37B spaceplane was photographed in orbit by a passing US-owned commercial satellite in 2024, and we finally have the image.
The Chinese spaceplane has delta wings, payload bay doors, a dark heat shield, and a rear-mounted service module with power-generating solar arrays. In other words, the design of the winged ship is, to a great degree, a copy of the X-37B spaceplane flown by the US Space Force.
The photo was taken by a commercial imaging satellite owned by a company called Vantor, known as Maxar in 2024. Vantor is one of several companies that provide reconnaissance imagery of locations around the world to the US military and US intelligence agencies. The same Earth-imaging satellites can point their telescopes at objects in space.
Lower-resolution views of a Chinese spaceplane showing the vehicle’s general shape were publicly available before the DIA assessment. A US Space Force official revealed Maxar’s observation at a 2024 conference in South Korea, but the Pentagon did not release the full-resolution image to the public until Monday, when it appeared in an unclassified Defense Intelligence Agency assessment of threats to the United States in space.
The DIA report doesn’t reveal much new about what the Chinese spaceplane does in orbit. China has launched four spaceplane missions since 2020 with durations of up to nine months. The fourth mission is in orbit today after launching in February. It is not publicly known whether China has one or more such spaceplanes in its inventory.
The Space Force has two X-37Bs flying in rotation, with the longest of their eight missions to date running two-and-a-half years from launch until landing. US officials have released photos of the X-37B vehicles, published information about their design and dimensions, and disclosed a handful of experiments they have carried into orbit. Most of the X-37B’s activities in space are classified.
Like the X-37B, China’s spaceplane lifts off inside the payload shroud of a conventional rocket, then operates as a satellite once in orbit. The spaceplane flies like a miniature unpiloted version of NASA’s Space Shuttle and reenters the atmosphere for an autonomous land runway landing at the end of each mission. Ground teams then refurbish it for another flight.
The “enhanced maneuverability” of spaceplanes make them “more suitable for certain missions than traditional satellites,” the DIA said in its report. So far, the Chinese spaceplane has only flown in low-Earth orbit (LEO) at an altitude of a few hundred miles. One of the Space Force’s X-37B flights soared to an altitude of more than 24,000 miles before using aerobraking to set up for reentry and landing .
Spaceplanes like China’s and the X-37B can also deploy small satellites from their cargo bay. Most recently, China demonstrated an ability to catch an object in orbit, perhaps using a robotic arm. The vehicle now in space released a sub-satellite in June and recaptured it in July, then did the same thing again in August and September, according to an analysis of open source orbital tracking data by Jonathan McDowell , an astrophysicist who catalogs spaceflight activity.
The official name of the Chinese spaceplane is even a mystery. It is often called Shenlong in Western publications, citing reports from the 2000s about China’s development of a robotic spaceplane. Chinese state media only refer to the vehicle as Chongfu Shiyong Shiyan Hangtian Qi, or CSSHQ, which means reusable experimental spacecraft, according to a fact sheet published by the Secure World Foundation .
The DIA did not disclose the exact circumstances of Maxar’s observation of the Chinese spaceplane, such as its timing, location, or distance, but Earth observations often use cameras to view other objects in space as their orbits intersect, an emerging field known as non-Earth imaging (NEI).
NEI allows commercial operators and government analysts to inspect satellites. This is especially useful for gleaning information about classified or proprietary satellite designs, extending a new avenue for international and corporate espionage to the high frontier.
The capability exhibited by Maxar and other commercial companies in the NEI field is distinct from the recent actions of some military spacecraft, such as Russia’s Kosmos 2612, which deliberately maneuvered to approach a US-registered radar imaging satellite earlier this month. Commercial NEI observations come from chance encounters, often at extremely high speed.
The DIA’s assessment of space threats includes an update on China’s pursuit of anti-satellite technology, or “counterspace” weapons. The intelligence agency reported the Chinese military likely considers directed-energy weapons (DEWs) “ideal counterspace systems” because they can be used to permanently or temporarily disable a satellite. One potential use for lasers in space would be to dazzle a sensor on an adversary’s satellite.
“China has multiple ground-based laser weapons with varying power levels to disrupt, degrade, or damage satellites in LEO,” the DIA said. “By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits.”
The DIA noted China’s testing of ground-based anti-satellite missiles and the country’s historic demonstration last year of satellite refueling in geosynchronous orbit, a regime some 22,000 miles (36,000 kilometers) over the equator, something no other country has achieved above LEO. China has also tested a robotic arm that could snag a spacecraft out of orbit, and now operates a growing fleet of satellites called TJS that routinely approach foreign spacecraft.
The US Space Force also has a constellation of inspector satellites in geosynchronous orbit and recently procured more that could be refueled, overcoming maneuverability limitations. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed last month that the Pentagon has fielded weapons in space , making the United States the first nation to acknowledge possession of orbital weapons.
Russia is pursuing its own orbital combat program, which includes an ambition to deploy a nuclear weapon in space, according to US intelligence officials.
A more conventional Russian weapons system, known as Nivelir, is designed to fire projectiles from one satellite to smash into another. The Russian military simulated an attack using the Nivelir system in 2020. In April, Russia launched a fleet of small satellites into an orbit close to a commercial radar remote sensing satellite owned by ICEYE that provides reconnaissance imagery to Ukraine. One of the Russian satellites moved within “tens of meters” of the ICEYE satellite earlier this month before backing away, US officials said.
